# Hybrid

`customer_support.offering.hybrid` · offering_family · parent `—`

> A product sold with the work that makes it useful: software plus implementation, a platform plus a managed team, hardware plus installation and maintenance. Hybrid is not a midpoint between the other two families and should not be modelled as one. It is the case where BOTH economics are live at once inside a single account, and where every ticket has to be sorted into one of them before it can be worked. That sorting decision is the whole discipline. A defect in the shared artefact is a product problem: reusable fix, aggregate view, one change retires the class. The identical symptom caused by this client's configuration, their data or the work we did for them is a service problem: bespoke labour, no aggregation, margin consumed by the hour. The symptom does not tell you which — the customer cannot know, and frequently neither can the first agent — and getting it wrong is expensive in both directions. Called product when it is service, the ticket sits waiting for a fix that will never ship because engineering correctly sees one affected customer. Called service when it is product, the account is billed or served for something that will recur across the install base and should have been fixed once. The second structural fact is that customers experience one vendor. They do not see the boundary between our platform and our people, and they will not accept it as an explanation. "That is a configuration issue, not a bug" is true, useless, and reliably the sentence that turns a ticket into an escalation. Both inherited habits fail here. The product operator aggregates everything and buries the bespoke half in an issue tracker where it starves. The services operator treats everything as bespoke and hand-answers forty instances of one defect. Hybrid support is defined by holding two dispositions at once and choosing between them early, explicitly, and out loud.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | a shared artefact plus per-client work that makes it fit; the client buys an outcome and receives both |
| pricing_shape | recurring licence or subscription plus services revenue — implementation, configuration, managed operations — usually on separate lines the customer reads as one |
| margin_profile | two margins in one account. The licence line behaves like a product and the services line is bounded by utilisation, so blended margin is meaningless and the split is the number that matters |
| post_sale_load | high and permanently mixed. Some post-signature work compounds across clients and some is consumed entirely by one, and the ratio between them is the health of the business |
| support_load | bimodal. A correlated product-shaped spike when the shared artefact breaks, and a steady uncorrelated service-shaped stream from configuration, data and integration work — reported through one queue and needing two treatments |
| resolution_locus | decided per ticket rather than per offering. Our codebase, this client's configuration, this client's data, a third-party integration, or work we did that has to be redone. Naming which one is the first act, and a queue that cannot record the answer cannot learn from it |
| notes | The practical test at ticket time is a counterfactual: would fixing this help the next client? If yes it is product, however bespoke it feels. If no it is service, however much it looks like a bug. That question is cheap, answerable in the first minute, and almost never asked.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `issue_ref`, `customer_account_ref`, `resolution_type`


> Both dimensions are mandatory here and each is optional in one of the parent families. issue_ref carries the product half and would be dead weight in a pure service queue; customer_account_ref carries the service half and is frequently absent in a pure product one. resolution_type is what records which way the sorting decision went, and a hybrid business that does not capture it cannot tell whether its support cost is compounding or evaporating.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `coverage_hours`


> Two entitlements in one account — the licence terms and the services agreement — with different clocks and different scopes. Customers reason about them as one, so the object has to hold both and support has to know which one a given ticket is being answered under before it promises anything.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.issue`

Requires `product_area_ref`


> The issue link is what makes the counterfactual answerable after the fact. Without it, "would fixing this have helped the next client?" can only be answered by opinion, and the product/service split degrades into whichever answer was commercially convenient.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> No deactivations, deliberately. Hybrid is the one family where every canonical capability has a genuine referent, because both economics are present — which is also why it is the hardest to run and the one where borrowed instincts do the most damage. The claim most worth arguing with is that the product/service sort should happen at triage rather than after diagnosis. Triage frequently lacks the information; the counterargument is that deferring the decision means it gets made implicitly by whoever picks the ticket up, which is worse than making it early and revising it.
